headlines.title: San Jose Police detain barricaded suspect, rescue two juveniles unharmed on Meadow Glen Way
headlines.description: An armed or barricade incident involving an adult male suspect and two juveniles in San Jose’s 1500 block of Meadow Glen Way concluded safely Tuesday morning after the suspect was taken into custody by police. The San Jose Police Department reported the active incident at 9:12 a.m., stating that officers responded to the residence for a welfare check. Upon arrival, authorities found that an adult male suspect had barricaded himself inside a home with two juveniles. Officers established a perimeter and began attempting to negotiate a peaceful surrender. The standoff ended successfully when the suspect was taken into custody and both juveniles were rescued unharmed. Further details regarding the suspect’s identity and potential charges have not yet been released as the investigation continues.

headlines.title: Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee addresses budget deficit, crime, and data center moratorium in State of the City
headlines.description: Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee laid out her vision for the city during her State of the City address, tackling some of Oakland’s biggest challenges—from public safety and illegal dumping to a budget deficit exceeding $100 million—while outlining how her administration plans to address those problems. Before Mayor Lee could address the state of Oakland, she walked past a crowd of city workers outside City Hall highlighting another major hurdle facing her administration. The city is dealing with a structural deficit of more than $100 million, and more than 1,000 funded positions remain unfilled, leaving remaining workers stretched thin. “What we really want to do is push against these high vacancy rates so we can have people doing the job of one person instead of two or three people,” said Julian Ware, an Oakland city worker and Local 21 vice president. Lee acknowledged the pressure, stating that her administration is working to improve services while addressing the city’s financial constraints. “We’re working hard on everything that you need to make the quality of life you deserve real,” Mayor Lee said. Inside City Council chambers, Lee turned to public safety. She pointed to declining crime, the end of federal oversight of the police department, and plans to recruit more officers through expanded police academies. However, she emphasized that reform does not end with the conclusion of federal monitoring. “The responsibility is ours now. Constitutional policing, civilian oversight must remain our standard,” Mayor Lee said. Lee also promised a more aggressive approach to one of Oakland’s most visible problems: illegal dumping. The city is allocating $9.2 million toward cleanup crews and technology designed to catch illegal dumpers in the act. “Let me be clear, illegal dumping is a moral disgrace,” Mayor Lee said. A new economic battleground is also emerging over the future of Oakland’s industries. Demonstrators are demanding a 45-day moratorium on proposed data centers, warning that the energy-intensive facilities could strain the city’s power supply and resources. “We’re talking about a technology that is threatening to destroy jobs, very energy hungry,” said Nicole Ghio, California director for Food & Water Watch. Mayor Lee expressed support for the moratorium, noting it will give residents more time to weigh in before any projects move forward. “Residents need to weigh in on any industry that’s trying to come to Oakland,” Mayor Lee said. While the mayor acknowledged that easy answers do not exist for every problem facing Oakland, she argued her administration has a concrete plan to keep the city moving in the right direction. “Oakland is definitely on the move, and together we’ll keep Oakland moving forward,” Mayor Lee said.

headlines.title: San Francisco sets strict robotaxi geofences to prevent Fleet Week gridlock
headlines.description: Fleet Week festivities began ramping up across San Francisco today, kicking off a packed schedule of at least 50 events spread across the city before the end of the weekend. From free music and ship tours to the iconic “angels in the sky,” the city is gearing up for more than a million visitors. With so much activity underway, city leaders are working to ensure crowds can navigate the celebrations without gridlock. The festivities got an early started Tuesday as the First Marine Division Brass Quintet opened a series of free concerts at Salesforce Park in downtown San Francisco, drawing a receptive lunchtime audience in the sunny weather. For some performers, the event is personal. “I’m a Bay Area native, originally,” said Staff Sgt. Alexandra Worley, a flutist and assistant conductor. “So it’s great to come back to San Francisco. And it’s great to see all the sights. And see the pride of the Bay.” The performance is just one of 50 that Navy and Marine musicians will put on over the next five days. Fleet Week organizers expect a strong rebound from last year’s events, when the U.S. Navy and Marines were absent due to a congressional budget standoff. To prevent a transportation meltdown similar to the gridlock seen during the July 4 fireworks display, city leaders are implementing strict traffic management plans. Starting Friday, the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency will geofence a large portion of the waterfront, barring autonomous vehicles from picking up or dropping off passengers in the area. Driverless taxis will also be restricted from entering the Presidio under the plan. “We’re always trying to improve,” Mayor Daniel Lurie said. “And so we’re working with the AV companies. SFMTA has added lines to make sure that traffic is not so congested.” Traditional taxis, rideshares, and private vehicles will still be permitted along the waterfront, alongside all public transportation. The autonomous vehicle restrictions will remain in effect from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Friday, Saturday, and Sunday. City resident Brennan Chapman is already putting together his weekend plans to watch the Blue Angels, and he agrees with keeping autonomous vehicles away from the waterfront crowds. “I think it will probably help with traffic,” Chapman said. “I think, especially when the crowds get bigger and bigger, Waymos have a harder time trying to figure out what to do, and they just sort of stop.”

headlines.title: Morgan Hill man accused of killing wife had prior arrests involving women
headlines.description: A man accused of killing his wife in Morgan Hill and then driving her to a San Jose hospital where he allegedly confessed to the crime has had previous run-ins with the law. Roy Anthony Lopez, 37, was previously arrested for two crimes, both against women, before he was taken into custody over the weekend on suspicion of killing his wife in their Morgan Hill home. Police said Lopez then drove more than 20 miles to Good Samaritan Hospital in San Jose with her body. “Our dispatch center received a call from San Jose Police Department advising that a male subject had drove into the parking lot of Good Samaritan Hospital and advised people in the area that he had killed his wife,” Morgan Hill police Sgt. Sean Bayard said. The woman was pronounced dead in the hospital parking lot. Investigators believe the fatal attack happened at the family home on Vintage Lane and said they believe the couple’s three children – ages 3, 6 and 14 – were there. According to court records, Lopez was arrested in November 2014 on suspicion of rape by force, but the charges were eventually dropped. In 2010, court documents show Lopez was arrested for battery against a spouse or cohabitant after a fight in a public place. In that case he was ultimately sentenced to volunteer work. Lopez now sits in a Santa Clara County jail while the district attorney’s office determines his charges. Steven Clark, a former prosecutor, said that’s likely to include a murder charge. “His admission to killing his wife will be the centerpiece of this case,” Clark said. Investigators have yet to release a cause of death but did say no gun was used. That could have an impact on charges. “The manner of the killing will be very important because he could later say, ‘Look, I didn’t intend to kill her. I drove her to the hospital. I didn’t want her to die,'” Clark said. Morgan Hill police said the couple had been married for more than 10 years. No restraining order had been filed against Lopez. If you or someone you know is experiencing domestic violence, contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline by calling 1-800-799-SAFE (7233), visiting www.thehotline.org or texting LOVEIS to 22522.

headlines.title: San Jose mayor seeks compromise in fight between food pantry, code enforcement
headlines.description: San Jose has threatened to close a food pantry over code violations, but Mayor Matt Mahan said Tuesday he’s working on a solution that would keep the operation running and quell the code concerns. Lighthouse Food Rescue and Distribution on North 17th Street has been fighting the city for a few days after code enforcement ordered it to shutter its food distribution due to zoning issues and threatened to fine the church behind the operation tens of thousands of dollars if it didn’t comply. There are also concerns that the sidewalk is being blocked by the operation. Mahan said he’s trying to find a compromise that works for all sides. “I just heard the news about the code action,” he said. “Look, in a big city, code enforcement can be a blunt instrument. They’re looking for code violations and trying to get people into compliance.” Lighthouse said it was stunned and troubled that its efforts to feed the community were at risk of being shuttered when the need is booming. “In the nonprofit world, we call this food deserts,” Pastor Ralph Olmos said. “These are places that are not occupied by any type of food rescue or distribution. So this is kind of a place that’s just kind of being ignored. It does ignore grandma and grandpa. It does ignore all our families that live in the community.” San Jose Oct 2 Sustainability Oct 5 San Francisco Sep 22 One proposal is moving the operation to city-owned property, with the city covering the cost of the move. “Our goal is to work with Pastor Olmos to find an appropriate place that is as close as possible to where he currently is operating and just make sure that that operation is in compliance with basic codes,” Mahan said. Olmos said it’s difficult to uproot the operation and set up shop somewhere else. “It depends,” Olmos said. “It depends where it’s at. I’m very tied into the northside. I don’t want to just leave people hanging.”

headlines.title: Not just truckers. How rising diesel prices are impacting everyday consumers
headlines.description: The cost of diesel fuel is hovering around record levels, especially in California. That doesn’t just mean more pain at the pump for drivers using diesel. It could affect how much consumers pay for just about anything on store shelves. That’s because no one feels the hit more directly than the trucking companies that deliver most of those goods to market. “It’s went up 45 to 50% since the beginning of the year,” JIT Transportation Executive Vice President Shane Salazar said. “These trucks have 100-gallon tanks, so just do the math. From $4.60 to $8.02, it’s simple math, but we have to manage it very tightly to just stay relevant and stay solvent.” JIT said candidly it has no choice but to pass some of the cost onto its customers. Oil & Gas Oct 5 Oil & Gas Oct 2 JIT is managing better than many other transportation companies nationwide. In some cases, independent truckers have been hit so hard by fuel price increases that they’ve started crowdfunding to fund their fill-ups. Gbenga Ajilore, chief economist for the research group Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, said the Iran war is at the heart of the rising costs. Ajilore said President Donald Trump’s recent order to allow commercial companies to use cheaper red-dyed diesel as well as deferring the federal highway diesel tax is not the answer. “The biggest issue is that we’ve had limited supply of crude oil from the conflict in the Middle East, so that’s caused prices to go up,” Ajilore said. “Unless you’re actually tackling the supply side of this issue, doing stuff on the demand side through taxes is not going to help.” California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s reaction was even more blunt. He said deferring that tax costs California money for transportation projects.

headlines.title: 2 dead, 2 injured after shootings, collision within minutes in Vallejo
headlines.description: Two shootings and one car crash within minutes of each other rocked Vallejo on Tuesday morning, leaving two people dead and two others injured. At approximately 8 a.m., a man was shot in the area of Castlewood Drive and Springs Road near Vallejo’s east side. The man was taken to a hospital by emergency personnel, where he is in critical condition, according to Vallejo police. Minutes later, at 8:15 a.m., two vehicles crashed in South Vallejo in the 1000 block of Sonoma Boulevard. One driver, a man, died from his injuries at the scene. The other driver was taken to a hospital and is expected to survive. At 8:23 a.m., a man was shot in the 200 block of Marin Street, just blocks away from the crash. The man was taken to a hospital, where he died from his wounds. Police have not confirmed whether either shooting or crash are related and did not provide further identifying information about the victims or suspected shooters. All three cases are under investigation, according to a spokesperson for the Vallejo Police Department. The city’s crisis response team, called IHART, along with a chaplain and officers are canvassing the affected areas to provide resources and trauma-informed care, police said.

headlines.title: Woman killed in suspected hit-and-run collision on I-680 in San Jose
headlines.description: A woman was struck and killed in a suspected hit-and-run collision on southbound Interstate 680 in San Jose late Monday night, according to the California Highway Patrol. Officers responded around 11 p.m. to the collision involving a pedestrian reported on southbound I-680 north of North Capitol Avenue. The woman, whose name has not been released, was pronounced dead at the scene, CHP officials said. Investigators determined that a vehicle struck her and the driver then fled. No description of the vehicle or driver was immediately available. The highway reopened as of early Tuesday morning. Anyone with information about the case is asked to call the CHP’s San Jose-area office at 408-961-0900.

headlines.title: Sonoma County declares local emergency ahead of expected El Niño flooding
headlines.description: Even before the first winter storm of the year, Sonoma County is declaring a local emergency in anticipation of above-average flooding expected from this season’s El Niño weather pattern. Sonoma County leaders are preparing for above-average rainfall from December through March. The National Weather Service is predicting a 70% chance that it will be the strongest El Niño in more than 70 years. The local emergency proclamation will help the county get an early start on staffing and training. There’s also a plan for community engagement, including a focus on people living in mobile homes near the lower Russian River. County crews will also continue preventive drainage clearing and road repairs. Sonoma County isn’t alone in preparing early. Two weeks ago, Gov. Gavin Newsom declared a statewide state of emergency to coordinate preparedness. The governor requested recommendations from the state’s environmental protection and natural resources agencies by Oct. 16.

headlines.title: ‘Horses and Heroes' brings new experience to SF Fleet Week
headlines.description: A new event is bringing service members out of the city and onto horseback. The first-of-its-kind Fleet Week event, called “Heroes and Horses,” is taking place at Ocean View Stables in Daly City. A couple dozen service members are participating, with some riding horses along a trail down to the beach. The experience grew out of the passion of a veteran-turned-business owner who found healing and purpose through horsemanship after his deployment to Afghanistan. The event comes as Fleet Week gets underway in San Francisco with traditional activities including the air show and ship tours. NBC Bay Area’s Ginger Conejero Saab has the full report in the video above.

headlines.title: Stanford scientist wins a Nobel Prize, then makes school lunches for his kids
headlines.description: Dr. Karl Deisseroth spent hours fielding congratulatory calls after learning early Monday that he had won a Nobel Prize for medicine for helping to open a new field of brain science called optogenetics. But it wasn’t long before the scientist asked for a break from all the attention for a more ordinary task: He needed to make school lunches for his children, who were asleep in the family home in Stanford, where their father had been speaking in the middle of the night with journalists and well-wishers. Deisseroth, 54, shared this year’s medicine prize with two researchers in Germany for their work in optogenetics, a field that combines light with genes to switch on and off neurons in living brains. A self-described night owl, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator and Stanford University professor often works past midnight. After reviewing papers and emailing his students, he said he had just gone to lie down when he got the call from the Nobel Assembly in Stockholm. “I almost felt as if I’d lost the power of forming words,” he told The Associated Press, “but I recovered after a minute or two.” He regained speech quickly enough for remote interviews with AP science reporters. Speedy emails with the Stanford communications staff had helped put them in touch. “No real sleep was achieved,” he said an hour after the announcement. As the science reporters chatted with Deisseroth over the phone and Zoom, an AP photographer and videographer raced to his home in Stanford. The photographer arrived around 3:30 a.m. to find Halloween decorations outside the home but just one light on inside. He was worried he had the wrong house before mustering the courage to knock on the door. Dr. Michelle Monje-Deisseroth, the scientist’s wife, answered and ushered the photographer into their home, where the Nobel winner was taking calls from the couch. Monje-Deisseroth, an HHMI investigator and Stanford pediatric neuro-oncologist, was at his side when she wasn’t making coffee for the Stanford communications staff who had joined the celebration. Deisseroth was surprised to hear his work had been honored with a Nobel Prize, he told the AP, but his wife was not. Deisseroth recounted the research he conducted with fellow Nobel winners Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, and its real-world impact. “For me, I’m a physician-scientist. I am a psychiatrist. I care about patients and my patients who have autism, who have depression,” he said. “I care about the hope that this brings. But I’m also a basic scientist, and I care about understanding this amazing organ, the brain, and how it works and how it integrates and computes and delivers all the things that make us human.” As Deisseroth wrapped up the interviews, he told the Stanford staff he needed an hourlong break beginning at 6:30 a.m. His kids would be waking up, he said, and they would need lunches before leaving for school. When one of the Stanford representatives wondered if the neighbors would mind all the late-night commotion, Monje-Deisseroth shrugged it off. They live in faculty housing, she said. There are a lot of Nobels in the neighborhood. __ Ramakrishnan reported from New York. Associated Press writers Stefanie Dazio in Berlin and Lauran Neergaard in Washington contributed to this report. ___ AP Nobel Prizes: https://apnews.com/hub/nobel-prizes
headlines.source: Noah Berger | The Associated Press, Terry Chea | The Associated Press and Adithi Ramakrishnan | The Associated Press

headlines.title: Berkeley candidates rally against surveillance technology
headlines.description: A group of candidates running for Berkeley City Council came together Tuesday morning to rally against surveillance technology outside City Hall. The seven candidates are opposing a City Council proposal involving license plate-reading cameras, drones and other surveillance technology. The candidates also say they are pledging to vote against mass surveillance and to remove the city’s Flock cameras. The candidates were joined by the former chair of the Police Accountability Board, which formally opposed the technology in 2023.
